headline: Medium-risk pair: shared document handling can leak or misroute content, while EMQX’s broad egress raises downstream compliance and cascade concerns.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: EMQX has broad network egress and pdf.js processes PDF files in a browser-based worker model, but no shared channel or direct ingestion path is documented. The only plausible bridge is manual transfer of PDF-derived content into EMQX workflows, so injection risk exists but is limited and not default.
conditions: IF an operator copies PDF text or annotations from pdf.js into EMQX-controlled inputs
IF EMQX treats imported text as instructions rather than data
mitigations: Require manual review of any PDF-derived text before reuse
Disable copy-paste of untrusted PDF content into operational prompts
Use a fixed template for EMQX inputs that strips instructions
requires-engineering: add provenance labels from pdf.js to downstream text

B_data_leakage.rationale: pdf.js handles PDF files locally, while EMQX touches IoT data and has broad network egress. If both are used on the same workstation or workspace, PDF contents can be moved into EMQX flows and then exfiltrated over the network. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default document-to-automation workflows.
conditions: IF PDF documents processed by pdf.js contain sensitive operational data
IF those contents are forwarded into EMQX inputs or logs
IF EMQX egress is enabled in the deployment
mitigations: Keep pdf.js and EMQX on separate workspaces
Redact sensitive fields before any handoff
Turn off EMQX outbound access where feasible
Review logs for accidental PDF content
requires-engineering: enforce content classification at the handoff boundary

C_capability_conflict.rationale: EMQX exposes HTTP API access and broad egress, while pdf.js supports browser-based tests and multiple instances. Their write surfaces do not overlap directly in the profiles, so there is no documented shared mutable resource or lock contention. Any conflict would require an external orchestrator not shown here.
conditions: IF an external orchestrator maps both agents onto the same writable directory
IF both agents are granted write access to the same mutable resource
mitigations: Assign separate directories per agent
Avoid concurrent writes to shared files
Serialize any handoff through a queue
requires-engineering: add locking around shared resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: pdf.js can produce extracted document content that EMQX may then consume through HTTP APIs or other workflows. Because EMQX has broad egress, downstream actions based on unverified PDF-derived content could propagate errors beyond the document layer. The profiles do not show verification gates between them, so the cascade is plausible.
conditions: IF EMQX consumes text or metadata extracted by pdf.js
IF no human or automated verification step checks the extracted content
mitigations: Add a verification step before EMQX acts on extracted text
Require human approval for high-impact actions
Log source document IDs alongside derived fields
requires-engineering: implement schema validation on pdf.js outputs

E_compliance.rationale: pdf.js processes PDF documents locally, while EMQX touches IoT data and can send data outward via broad network egress. If regulated or sensitive PDF content is routed into EMQX, retention and residency obligations can diverge across the pair. No compliance controls are documented here, so the mismatch risk is moderate rather than proven severe.
conditions: IF PDF documents contain regulated personal or operational data
IF EMQX stores, forwards, or logs that data outside the required jurisdiction
mitigations: Classify documents before processing
Block regulated PDFs from EMQX handoff
Set short log retention on EMQX
Review data-flow documentation
requires-engineering: add residency controls to the pipeline
